name: OONI Probe CLI / probe-engine
purpose: Command-line network-measurement client implementing OONI's test suite — web connectivity, instant-messaging apps, circumvention tools, performance — which uploads results to OONI's collector for publication as open data.
journalism_use_case: A reporter or local stringer runs ooniprobe from inside the affected country to generate timestamped, independently published evidence that specific news sites or messaging apps are being blocked, and what technique is doing the blocking (DNS tampering, TCP reset, TLS interference). That published measurement is citable in the story.
pros: Produces third-party-verifiable evidence: because results are published to OONI's open dataset with a permalink, a story can cite the measurement rather than asserting a block
Identifies the blocking technique, not just the fact of a block — which is what distinguishes a state-ordered DNS block from a site outage in print
Very actively maintained (v3.31.1, 2026-11-03; pushed 2026-11-17) with institutional backing and a clean issue ratio
GPL-3.0, cross-platform Go binaries, scriptable for repeated measurement over time
cons: Running probes is legally and physically risky for the operator in repressive jurisdictions — measurement traffic is distinguishable and the ASN and network name are published with the result, which can narrow down who ran it
Results detect anomalies, not intent: confirming a block usually needs corroboration across probes, networks and time, and single measurements are routinely over-read
Requires GeoIP databases and OONI's collector and test-helper infrastructure, so it is not a standalone tool
Coverage is only what someone chose to test — a country can look unblocked because nobody ran a probe there
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: OONI's measurement corpus is used in published reporting and in advocacy submissions, and the project itself documents that results are published with ASN and network name — the key operational-security fact. 301 stars, 40 open issues, release 2026-11-03.
assessment: Essential to this pillar and the thing I would reach for first on a 'is the site blocked' question — but the risk sits with the person running it, not with you. For media-in-exile work the responsible pattern is: never ask an in-country source to run a probe without explaining that the ASN and network are published; prefer existing OONI Explorer data where it already covers the network; and where you do commission measurement, corroborate across time and networks before publishing an attribution.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.31.1 (2026-11-03), 301 stars, 40 open issues. Frequent versioned releases, same-day commits, funded institutional maintainer with a security process.
model_or_data_licence: Published OONI measurement data is open data (CC0-style per OONI's policy — verify the current terms before bulk redistribution). The Citizen Lab test lists that drive testing are CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, which is a separate and more restrictive licence.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the client limits embedding in proprietary tooling. Note the test lists' NonCommercial clause if you redistribute them alongside results.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. The real cost is risk borne by the person running the probe, and the time to interpret results correctly.
privacy: Measurement results are uploaded by default to OONI's collector and then published as open data including the probe's ASN, network name and country. This is deliberate — the value is public evidence — but it means the measurement is not private, and in a small network the ASN can be identifying. Treat running a probe as a public act.
alternatives: OONI Explorer first, to check whether existing measurements already answer the question without new risk
RIPE Atlas tooling for reachability and routing measurement from volunteer probes
IODA for country-level outage confirmation without in-country action
blockers: Operator risk in repressive jurisdictions; ASN and network name are published with results

name: OONI Probe Multiplatform
purpose: Kotlin Multiplatform app for Android, iOS and desktop that runs the OONI test suite with a graphical interface and publishes results to OONI's collector.
journalism_use_case: Newsrooms can ask sources, correspondents or volunteer networks inside a country to install one app and run a standard test suite, producing comparable public measurements without any command-line skills — the practical route to building coverage of whether your own outlet is blocked across several ISPs.
pros: Removes the technical barrier entirely, which is what makes distributed measurement by non-technical volunteers possible at all
Standardised test suite means results from different volunteers are directly comparable and aggregate into a usable dataset
Very active (v6.3.1, 2026-11-09; pushed 2026-11-17) and consolidating previously separate Android/iOS codebases into one maintained project
App-store distribution means volunteers do not need to trust a sideloaded binary
cons: Still an app the user must deliberately install and run, so coverage is opportunistic and biased toward activist and technical populations — the networks used by ordinary readers are under-sampled
Installing and running a censorship-measurement app is itself a risk signal on a user's device in a repressive country, and the app's presence may be visible to someone inspecting the phone
The older Android codebase is archived, so bug reports and older documentation point at dead code
Results publish ASN, network name and country, so a volunteer on a small or identifiable network is not anonymous
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the consolidation of previously separate platform codebases into probe-multiplatform (the older Android repository being archived), and the app's own disclosure that results are published as open data with network metadata. 99 stars, 32 open issues, release 2026-11-09.
assessment: The right tool for commissioning distributed measurement, with a serious duty of care attached. For your profile I would (1) brief volunteers explicitly that the app is visible on their device and that their network is published, (2) prefer volunteers outside high-risk categories where possible, and (3) treat coverage gaps as evidence of nothing rather than evidence of no blocking. Used carefully it is how a small outlet can demonstrate that it is being blocked across multiple ISPs.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v6.3.1 (2026-11-09), 99 stars, 32 open issues. Current releases on a 6.x line; the deliberate consolidation of platform codebases is evidence of active engineering investment.
model_or_data_licence: Measurement data published as OONI open data; Citizen Lab test lists are CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0; app-store distribution of GPL software has known friction on iOS — relevant only if you fork and redistribute.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Cost is volunteer coordination and the duty-of-care briefing time.
privacy: Results upload to OONI's collector and are republished as open data with ASN, network name and country. The app surfaces this, but a volunteer may not grasp the implication — explaining it is your responsibility. The app's presence on a device is itself a disclosure in a hostile-search scenario.
alternatives: OONI Explorer to use existing measurements without asking anyone to take risk
OONI Probe CLI for technically capable operators needing scripted repetition
IODA for country-level outage evidence with no in-country participation
blockers: Volunteer risk: app presence on device plus published network metadata

name: OONI Explorer
purpose: Web interface over OONI's measurement archive, providing per-country and per-network views of blocked sites and apps, anomaly and confirmed-blocking classifications, and permalinks to individual measurements.
journalism_use_case: The fastest route from 'is this site blocked in country X' to a citable, linkable public measurement. The per-measurement permalinks are usable directly as sourcing in a published story, which is rare — most network evidence cannot be cited by a reader.
pros: Citable permalinks are the decisive feature: a reader or a lawyer can open the exact measurement your story relies on
Requires no technical skill and no risk — browsing is read-only and runs no measurement from your machine
Covers a long time series, so you can show when blocking started rather than only that it exists
Maintained alongside the rest of the OONI stack with current commits
cons: Shows anomalies and confirmed-blocking classifications, not a verdict on who ordered a block — attribution is a reporting task, not a data lookup
Low-coverage countries and networks can look quiet simply because nobody ran a probe there, and this absence is easy to misread as absence of censorship
Release metadata is stale (v2.1.0 from 2020-10-20 against tag v2.6.1), so the published release objects understate maintenance
96 open issues; the UI is functional rather than polished for non-expert interpretation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the service is live and widely cited in censorship reporting and advocacy; the repository shows current commits (pushed 2026-11-17) alongside stale release objects, which is a release-hygiene artefact rather than a maintenance signal.
assessment: Start here on any blocking question — it costs nothing and risks nobody, and often answers the question outright. The discipline to impose on yourself and your reporters: never write 'not blocked' from an empty Explorer result, because coverage gaps are the norm in exactly the countries that matter. Where coverage is missing, that is when commissioning a probe becomes worth its risk.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release object v2.1.0 (2020-10-20) but latest tag v2.6.1, 95 stars, 96 open issues. Judged on commit recency and the live service rather than release objects, which are not maintained for this front end.
model_or_data_licence: Displays OONI open measurement data; verify OONI's current data terms before bulk reuse.
costs: Free to use. Self-hosting the front end is possible but pointless for most users since the data is OONI's. No cost.
privacy: Reads and displays already-public measurement data; browsing is read-only and no measurement runs from your browser. Your browsing of Explorer is visible to OONI's hosting in the ordinary way — consider Tor if even the query pattern is sensitive.
alternatives: OONI Probe CLI/app where coverage is missing and new measurement is justified
IODA for outage-level rather than site-level evidence
Internet Society Pulse for a quick summary figure — but with unverified reuse terms

name: OONI backend
purpose: Server-side components of the OONI system: the measurements API, the collector that receives probe submissions, and the test helpers that probes use to distinguish network interference from ordinary failure.
journalism_use_case: Data teams query the OONI measurements API to pull structured blocking counts per country, ASN and URL over time for charts and trend reporting, instead of hand-collecting from the web interface — the route from anecdote to a quantified story about press blocking.
pros: The measurements API is the practical deliverable for a newsroom data team: structured, filterable, open access to a decade of censorship measurement
BSD-3-Clause and actively developed (pushed 2026-11-17), with the API documented and stable enough to build dashboards against
Test-helper architecture is what makes OONI's blocking classifications defensible, so understanding it helps you interpret the data honestly
cons: Operationally heavy to self-host and not meant as a desktop tool — in practice you consume the hosted API rather than run this
Two older repositories in this lineage are archived or dormant, so older tutorials point at dead code — a real navigation problem
Release objects are badly stale (v1.3.6 from 2019-03-26) with 198 open issues, so the repository is hard to assess from metadata alone
Querying the hosted API discloses your research interest to OONI's infrastructure
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 198 open issues and release objects seven years old against current commits — a repository where metadata signals mislead and the live API is the real artefact. 60 stars.
assessment: Treat the API as the product and this repository as its documentation. For your profile the useful work is a small internal client that pulls per-country, per-ASN blocking counts for the outlets you care about and charts them over time — that is a publishable monitoring capability built in a day. Self-hosting the backend is not something I would recommend; there is no benefit over querying OONI unless you are running an independent measurement network.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.3.6 (2019-03-26), 60 stars, 198 open issues. Current commits with abandoned release tagging; the live API's operation is the stronger evidence. Noted that sibling repositories in this lineage are archived.
model_or_data_licence: OONI measurement data is published as open data; confirm current terms for bulk redistribution.
costs: No fee to use the hosted API. Self-hosting would require ClickHouse/PostgreSQL-class stores and significant ops — not recommended. Estimate.
privacy: The hosted API ingests probe submissions including ASN, network name and country and republishes them as open data. As a consumer, your queries are visible to OONI's infrastructure.
alternatives: OONI Data (oonidata/oonipipeline) for bulk dataset construction rather than API queries
OONI Explorer for one-off human lookups
Censored Planet's published BigQuery tables for an independent measurement source

name: OONI Data (oonidata / oonipipeline)
purpose: Tooling to download OONI's raw measurement archive in bulk and transform it into analysis-ready observation tables, with a pipeline component targeting an analytics data store.
journalism_use_case: The tool to reach for when a story needs a country-wide or multi-year blocking dataset rather than individual measurements — for example reconstructing exactly when a set of news domains started being tampered with across every ISP in a country.
pros: Bulk access is qualitatively different from API queries: it lets you do the longitudinal analysis that produces a 'when did this start' finding
Derives structured observation tables, so the hard interpretive work of turning raw measurements into comparable rows is already done
Actively developed (pushed 2026-11-16) with a current tag line (v5.1.0)
cons: GitHub reports no licence for this repository because the root has no LICENSE file — the BSD-3-Clause text sits in the oonidata/ and oonipipeline/ subpackages, so repo-level licence clarity is poor and a compliance reviewer will flag it
Release objects are badly stale (v0.2.3 from 2022-11-14 against tag v5.1.0), so versioning signals are confusing
Requires bulk object storage for the measurement archive and a ClickHouse-class analytics store for the pipeline — real infrastructure
Tiny community (11 stars, 31 open issues); you will be reading source
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the root-level licence gap with BSD-3-Clause text present only in subpackages (verified session 1, retained); the release-versus-tag discrepancy; 11 stars.
assessment: Worth the effort only for a specific longitudinal story, and I would plan it as a project rather than a tool: provision storage, pull the archive for the countries and date range you need, build the observation tables, then analyse in DuckDB or ClickHouse. Resolve the licence question by citing the subpackage LICENSE files explicitly in your compliance notes — the code is BSD-3-Clause, the repository packaging is just untidy.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.2.3 (2022-11-14), latest tag v5.1.0, SPDX none at root, 11 stars, 31 open issues. Current commits and tag progression under institutional maintenance; release objects abandoned.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (in the oonidata/ and oonipipeline/ subpackages; the repository root has NO LICENSE file, so GitHub reports none)
model_or_data_licence: OONI measurement data published as open data; confirm current terms for redistribution.
licence_restrictions: Code is BSD-3-Clause per subpackage licence files, but the missing root LICENSE is a compliance-review irritant — document the subpackage paths if your legal team requires it.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: bulk object storage for the archive (tens to hundreds of GB depending on scope) plus an analytics store. Estimate; assumes self-hosted ClickHouse or cloud equivalent.
privacy: Pulls already-public OONI measurements to local or cloud storage; no new measurement is performed, so no risk to anyone in-country. Your download pattern is visible to OONI's storage provider.
alternatives: OONI measurements API for smaller, targeted queries
Censored Planet's published BigQuery tables for an independent longitudinal source
IODA for outage timelines rather than per-URL blocking

name: Citizen Lab URL test lists
purpose: Curated per-country and global lists of URLs categorised by topic (news media, human rights, political criticism, LGBT, circumvention tools) that drive censorship-measurement testing.
journalism_use_case: Defines what gets tested, so a newsroom can check whether the outlets it cares about are even in the list for a country — and submit them if not — before citing OONI coverage as evidence of press blocking. If your outlet is not on the list, nobody has been testing whether you are blocked.
pros: Directly actionable: adding your own domains via pull request means future OONI measurements will test them, turning a coverage gap into evidence over time
Topic categorisation lets you make statements about classes of censorship (news media versus circumvention tools) rather than single sites
Maintained with real community input (pushed 2026-11-04, 554 stars, active PR flow)
Static data in git, so it is trivially auditable and versioned — you can show what the list contained on a given date
cons: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0: the NonCommercial clause is a genuine problem for commercial newsrooms wanting to redistribute the lists or build products on them, and ShareAlike propagates to derived lists — legal review is warranted
There is no LICENSE file in the repository root (GitHub reports no SPDX), so the licence is asserted in documentation rather than detected — an extra verification step for your compliance records
148 open issues, many of them pending list submissions, so inclusion is not immediate
List composition reflects curatorial judgement, and under-coverage of a country's independent media is a real and consequential gap
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 licence and the absence of a root LICENSE file (verified session 1, retained); 148 open issues including submission backlog; 554 stars.
assessment: Do two things with this: check whether your own and partner outlets' domains are listed for the countries you care about, and submit them if not — that is a concrete, cheap action that improves the evidence base for your own future reporting. Then handle the licence carefully: reading and acting on the list is fine, redistributing it or building a commercial product on it is not, and 'we are a newsroom' does not satisfy NonCommercial.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-04, no releases (git-tracked data), SPDX none, 554 stars, 148 open issues. Continuous community contributions with institutional curation by Citizen Lab; the open-issue count is largely submission queue rather than defects.
licence: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (asserted in project documentation; no LICENSE file in the repository root and GitHub reports no SPDX)
model_or_data_licence: Same — this is a dataset, not software.
licence_restrictions: NonCommercial bars commercial redistribution or productisation; ShareAlike requires derived lists to carry the same licence. A commercially operated newsroom cannot assume its use is non-commercial. Reading and testing against the lists is ordinary use; republishing them is not.
costs: No fee. No infrastructure. Cost is the effort of submitting additions and tracking whether they are merged.
privacy: Static public data in git; no measurement or personal data involved. Note that submitting your outlet's domains is a public act that signals interest in its censorship status.
alternatives: OONI's own category definitions for understanding what coverage means
Maintaining a private internal list for your own direct testing, avoiding the NC licence entirely
Commissioning targeted measurement of specific domains via OONI Probe
blockers: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 NonCommercial clause — blocks commercial redistribution and productisation

name: IODA (Internet Outage Detection and Analysis)
purpose: System that detects and visualises internet outages by combining three independent signals — BGP routing withdrawals, active ICMP probing of address space, and background radiation observed at a network telescope — at country, region and ASN granularity.
journalism_use_case: The standard first stop for confirming and timestamping a national or regional internet shutdown, because agreement across three unrelated signals is hard to explain away as a measurement artefact — which is exactly the standard a shutdown story needs to survive official denial.
pros: Triangulation across three independent signal types is the methodological strength: a shutdown visible in BGP, active probing and telescope data simultaneously is very strong evidence
Country and ASN granularity lets you say which operator went dark and when, which is the attribution-relevant detail
Hosted dashboard requires no technical skill and no in-country action, so there is no risk to anyone
Actively operated (pushed 2026-11-16) with institutional backing at Georgia Tech
cons: The LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies grants use for academic research and education without fee and directs other uses to contact the university — so despite public code this is NOT open source for a commercial newsroom
Release objects are stale (v1.0.0 from 2024-02-21) and the repository has 59 open issues with only 3 stars — the hosted service is the real artefact and the code is hard to assess
Measures reachability, not cause: it shows that address space became unreachable, not who ordered it or why — attribution remains reporting work
Self-hosting is impractical: it requires BGP collector feeds, probeable address space and a darknet telescope, which no newsroom has
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the academic-research-and-education licence text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies (verified session 1, retained); 59 open issues; v1.0.0 release from February 2024. IODA is widely cited in shutdown reporting and advocacy, which is credible usage evidence for the hosted dashboard.
assessment: Use the hosted dashboard freely for confirming and timestamping shutdowns — that is its purpose and it is excellent at it. Do not plan to self-host or to build a product on the code, because the licence directs non-academic use to the university. For your profile the practical combination on a shutdown story is IODA for the timestamp and the affected ASNs, PyBGPStream for independently reconstructing the route withdrawals, and OONI for what was blocked rather than merely unreachable.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v1.0.0 (2024-02-21), SPDX NOASSERTION (actual: academic-use licence), 3 stars, 59 open issues. The hosted service is continuously operated and the UI repository receives current commits; institutional maintenance at Georgia Tech.
licence: NOT OSS — academic research and education use without fee; other uses directed to contact the university (LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies)
model_or_data_licence: Published IODA data terms were not separately verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Commercial use of the code requires contacting the university. Using the public dashboard and citing it in reporting is ordinary use of a public service; redistributing the code or data commercially is not covered.
costs: Free to use the dashboard. Self-hosting is impractical (BGP feeds, probeable address space, a network telescope). No realistic infrastructure estimate because the architecture is not reproducible by a newsroom.
privacy: Aggregates network-level public measurement data to country, region and ASN granularity; it observes reachability of address space rather than individuals. Using the dashboard runs no measurement from your machine and exposes no one in-country.
alternatives: PyBGPStream to independently reconstruct BGP withdrawals from public archives
OONI Explorer for what was blocked rather than unreachable
Internet Society Pulse or Cloudflare Radar for quick summary figures, with their own terms
blockers: Academic-use licence on the code — not usable as commercial newsroom infrastructure (the public dashboard is fine to use and cite)

name: PyBGPStream / libbgpstream
purpose: Python bindings over libBGPStream for streaming and analysing historical and near-real-time BGP routing data from RouteViews and RIPE RIS collectors.
journalism_use_case: Lets a data journalist independently reconstruct which ASNs withdrew which prefixes, and at what minute, during a shutdown — the evidence that distinguishes an operator-executed disconnection from a transit failure, and that survives a government's claim of a technical fault.
pros: Gives you primary-source routing evidence rather than someone else's dashboard, which is what you need when a finding will be officially denied
BSD-2-Clause, so the analysis code and methodology can be published alongside a story with no licence friction
Reads public archives only — no probing, no user data, no risk to anyone in-country
Minute-level granularity on route withdrawals is often the sharpest timestamp available for a shutdown
cons: Build and dependency setup is genuinely fiddly (libbgpstream, wandio, librdkafka C toolchain) and is where most people give up
Release cadence is slow: last tagged release v2.0.4 in February 2024, with the last push 2026-07-06
BGP shows control-plane intent: routes can remain announced while the data plane is blocked, so BGP silence proves disconnection but BGP presence does not prove connectivity
Interpreting collector data correctly (peer visibility, prefix aggregation, collector outages) requires real expertise and is easy to get wrong in public
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 45 stars with 22 open issues, last tagged release 2024-02-20, last push 2026-07-06. CAIDA's BGPStream is a standard instrument in network-measurement research, which is strong adjacent-field credibility.
assessment: Worth the setup cost once, and then it is a durable capability: shutdown stories recur and this is the independent evidence layer. For your profile I would containerise it so the build pain is paid once, and pair it with IODA — IODA to find the event quickly, PyBGPStream to reconstruct it from primary data for publication. Have someone who understands BGP review the interpretation before it goes in print; the failure mode here is a confident wrong claim about which operator did what.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-06, latest release v2.0.4 (2024-02-20), 45 stars, 22 open issues. Four months since last push and over two years since a release; a mature research library with slow but non-zero maintenance under institutional ownership.
model_or_data_licence: RouteViews and RIPE RIS MRT archives are public data under their respective providers' terms (not separately verified here).
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: compute and disk for MRT archive processing — a shutdown-window analysis is modest, a multi-month study is substantial. Estimate.
privacy: Reads public routing-table and update archives; no probing and no user data. One of the safest instruments in this pillar from an operational-security standpoint.
alternatives: IODA for a faster, no-setup answer — but academic licence on the code
RIPE Atlas tooling for active reachability measurement alongside routing data
RIPEstat APIs for simpler one-off routing lookups

name: Censored Planet data analysis pipeline
purpose: Pipeline that processes Censored Planet's raw remote-measurement data (Hyperquack, Satellite/Iris) into analysis tables published in BigQuery, covering network interference across roughly 200 countries without in-country probes.
journalism_use_case: Underpins global, longitudinal blocking comparisons across around 200 countries without anyone having to run a probe inside a censored network — which matters precisely when in-country testing would be unsafe for the person doing it.
pros: Remote measurement removes operator risk entirely, making it the ethically preferable source when you cannot ask anyone in-country to take a risk
Global and longitudinal by design, so cross-country comparisons are methodologically consistent rather than assembled from disparate sources
Apache-2.0 with published BigQuery tables, so the analytical deliverable is directly queryable
Academic provenance with published methodology, so findings can be defended and cited
cons: Not runnable by a newsroom in practice — it is a GCP-based pipeline over data you do not hold; treat the published BigQuery tables and raw releases as the deliverable and this repository as methodological documentation
Remote-measurement techniques infer blocking from outside the network, so they are weaker than in-country measurement on some interference types and carry their own false-positive modes
Last push 2025-06-29 with no releases and 20 stars — the pipeline repository is lightly maintained even while the data programme continues
Using the BigQuery tables means a Google Cloud account and query costs, which is a paid dependency
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: last push 2025-06-29, no releases, 20 stars, 13 open issues; Apache-2.0; dependency on GCP and on censoredplanet/assets-censoredplanet for blockpage fingerprints. Censored Planet's published research is well established in the measurement literature.
assessment: Use the published data, not the code. For your profile the decisive advantage over OONI is ethical rather than technical: it answers blocking questions without putting a person in a hostile jurisdiction at risk, which should make it your first option when the alternative is asking a source to run a probe. Budget for BigQuery query costs and have a methodologist check the inference limits before you publish a country comparison.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-06-29, no releases or tags, 20 stars, 13 open issues. Seventeen months since last push. The research programme and data publication continue, so the pipeline code is stable rather than abandoned — but the repository alone is weak evidence either way, hence the cautious classification.
model_or_data_licence: Published Censored Planet data terms were not separately verified in this survey; check before bulk redistribution.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. Data terms unverified here.
costs: No software fee. Querying the published BigQuery tables incurs Google Cloud charges based on bytes scanned — a real, usage-based cost that scales with how broadly you query (current BigQuery rates not verified in this survey). Raw data releases can be downloaded instead, trading cloud cost for storage and compute.
privacy: Processes already-published remote-measurement data about network behaviour. The measurement technique probes infrastructure from outside, so no individual in-country is involved or exposed. Your BigQuery queries are visible to Google.
alternatives: OONI data where in-country measurement exists and is safe
IODA for outage rather than blocking questions
CenAlert for early-warning signals derived partly from this data

name: CenAlert
purpose: Research prototype that combines aggregate public search-interest signals with censorship-measurement data to raise early alerts that a country may have begun censoring a topic, pushing notifications to Slack.
journalism_use_case: Points toward an early-warning tripwire — being told a country may have started censoring a topic before a story breaks — rather than confirming a block after the fact. For an exile outlet, early notice that your own topic area is being filtered is operationally valuable.
pros: Addresses the right problem: existing tools confirm censorship retrospectively, and the newsworthy moment is when it starts
GPL-3.0 and recently active (pushed 2026-11-17), so the approach is inspectable and current
Architecturally simple — configuration plus a Slack webhook — so the concept is cheap to reimplement if the prototype does not suit
cons: A paper-accompanying prototype with almost no external users (3 stars), thin documentation and no packaging — this is research code, not a tool
Alerts are probabilistic hints that must be verified against OONI or IODA before publication; an alert alone is not a finding
Requires Google Trends access, a Slack token and per-topic/per-country configuration in a shell script — brittle, and Google Trends access terms and stability are outside your control
Narrow Python version support (3.8-3.12) and no release engineering
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 3 stars means there is no community signal, which I note rather than inflate. The approach is published research from a credible measurement group; the implementation is a prototype by the project's own framing.
assessment: Take the idea, not the code. The concept — correlate a drop in search interest or a measurement anomaly with a topic you care about and get alerted — is worth building properly for the countries your outlet covers, and it is a few days of work against the OONI API plus a simple baseline. CenAlert's value to you is as a published method and a Slack-alert pattern. Any alert must be corroborated before it informs reporting.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, no releases or tags, 3 stars, 0 open issues. Current commits from the research group but no packaging, documentation maturity or community. Classified stable-low: active hands, prototype status.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 limits embedding in proprietary tooling; irrelevant for internal use.
costs: No fee. Requires Google Trends access (terms and rate limits outside your control; not priced here) and a Slack workspace. Minimal compute.
privacy: Consumes aggregate public search-interest signals and censorship-measurement data and pushes alerts to a Slack workspace. No individual data; note that your topic and country configuration reveals your editorial interests to Google Trends and to Slack.
alternatives: A custom alerting job against the OONI measurements API for the domains you care about
IODA's own alerting for outage-level events
Censored Planet BigQuery tables with a scheduled query and threshold
